prompt: In what form are the alkali metals found in nature?

choices.text: As +1 cations in minerals such as rock salt (NaCl) and natron (Na2CO3·10H2O)
As the free metals, since they are unreactive
choices.why: Alkali metals are powerful reductants, so they don't survive as free metals in the oxidizing environment at Earth's surface.

choices.text: As −1 anions in salts
choices.why: Alkali metal anions (like sodide) can be made in the lab, but in nature the metals occur as +1 cations.

choices.text: As +2 cations in carbonate minerals
choices.why: Alkali metals form +1 cations. The +2 state is typical of the alkaline earth metals.

explanation: Alkali metals are powerful reductants and do not exist as free metals in the relatively oxidizing environment at Earth's surface. They are found as +1 cations in minerals like rock salt (halite, NaCl) and natron (Na2CO3·10H2O), so the free metals are made by reducing these cations.

prompt: In the Downs process, 2 NaCl(l) → 2 Na(l) + Cl2(g). Why must the cathode and anode be carefully separated in the Downs cell?

choices.text: To prevent the explosively exothermic reaction between the molten sodium and chlorine gas products
To stop the NaCl from melting
choices.why: The salt is deliberately melted so the ions can move to the electrodes.

choices.text: Because sodium is denser than molten NaCl and would sink onto the anode
choices.why: Sodium is less dense than molten NaCl, so it floats to the top and collects above the cathode.

choices.text: Because the cell runs on aqueous NaCl, and water must be kept from the anode
choices.why: The Downs process electrolyzes molten NaCl, not an aqueous solution.

explanation: The salt is melted so cations can move to the cathode and anions to the anode. Because sodium is reactive, the cell must keep the metal away from the anode products: Cl2 bubbles out of the cell, and the sodium, being less dense than molten NaCl, floats up and collects above the cathode. This prevents the explosively exothermic reaction of Na with Cl2.

prompt: Potassium can be made by reducing potassium halides with calcium carbide: 2 KX + CaC2 → 2 K + CaX2 + 2 C. How many moles of potassium are produced from 0.75 mol CaC2 with excess KX?
explanation: The equation gives 2 mol K per mol CaC2, so 0.75 mol CaC2 × 2 = 1.5 mol K. Potassium can also be made by reducing KCl with Na or K2CO3 with carbon.

prompt: Why do alkali metals melt and boil at much lower temperatures than most other metals?

choices.text: Their few valence electrons and relatively low effective nuclear charges make their metallic bonding weak
They are held together by covalent bonds rather than metallic bonds
choices.why: Alkali metals are held together by metallic bonding, which is weak because they have few valence electrons and low effective nuclear charges.

choices.text: They have very high ionization energies
choices.why: Alkali metals have low ionization energies. Their weak metallic bonding comes from few valence electrons and low Z*.

choices.text: Their atoms get smaller down the group
choices.why: Atoms get larger down the group, which weakens metallic bonding further and lowers the melting points.

explanation: Compared to other metals, alkali metals have few valence electrons and relatively low effective nuclear charges, so their metallic bonds are weaker. They melt and boil at low temperatures (Cs melts at 28 °C), are soft enough to cut with a spatula, and their melting and boiling points decrease down the group as atomic size increases.

prompt: Ionization energies fall from Li (513 kJ/mol) to Cs (376 kJ/mol), yet Li is the most reducing alkali metal in water. Which data best explain this?

choices.text: The hydration enthalpy of Li^+ (−1091 kJ/mol) is far more negative than that of Na^+ (−515) or Cs^+ (−296), so Li^+ is strongly stabilized in solution
Lithium has the lowest ionization energy of the group
choices.why: Lithium has the highest ionization energy of the alkali metals. The strong hydration of Li^+ is what makes it the best reductant.

choices.text: The hydration enthalpies of all the alkali metal cations are nearly equal
choices.why: They differ hugely: Li^+ is −1091 kJ/mol and Cs^+ only −296 kJ/mol.

choices.text: Cesium's larger radius makes Cs^+ more strongly hydrated
choices.why: Larger cations are less strongly hydrated. The small Li^+ ion has by far the most negative hydration enthalpy.

explanation: Cation formation is favored by low ionization energies and by high solvation energies of the cations. Down the group the solvation energy falls far more steeply than the ionization energy, with most of that drop from Li^+ to Na^+. The great stability of Li^+ in solution makes Li the most reducing alkali metal. Na is the least reducing, and K, Rb, and Cs have about the same reduction potentials.

prompt: The hydration (solvation) enthalpy of Li^+ is −1091 kJ/mol and that of Cs^+ is −296 kJ/mol. By what percentage does the magnitude of the hydration enthalpy decrease from Li^+ to Cs^+?
explanation: Percent decrease = (1091 − 296)/1091 × 100% = 795/1091 × 100% = 72.9%. This steep drop in cation solvation energy, much larger than the change in ionization energy, is why Li^+ is so much more stabilized in water than the heavier alkali metal cations.

prompt: All alkali metals react with water: 2 M(s) + 2 H2O(l) → 2 M^+ + 2 OH^− + H2(g). How does the vigor of the reaction change down the group?

choices.text: Li usually just fizzes, Na and K usually give a colored flame, and Rb and Cs explode
Li explodes while Cs only fizzes
choices.why: It's the reverse: lithium usually just fizzes, and the reactions of Rb and Cs are explosive.

choices.text: Only Li and Na react; K, Rb, and Cs do not
choices.why: All of the alkali metals react vigorously with water.

choices.text: All react equally gently without igniting the H2
choices.why: The reactions are exothermic and often ignite the hydrogen; Rb and Cs explode.

explanation: The reactions are all exothermic and often lead to combustion of the H2 produced. Lithium usually just fizzes, Na and K usually give a colored flame, and Rb and Cs react explosively.

prompt: Sodium reacts with water: 2 Na(s) + 2 H2O(l) → 2 Na^+ + 2 OH^− + H2(g). How many moles of H2 are produced when 0.36 mol Na reacts completely?
explanation: The equation gives 1 mol H2 per 2 mol Na, so 0.36 mol Na × (1 mol H2 / 2 mol Na) = 0.18 mol H2.

prompt: A small amount of sodium is dissolved in dry liquid ammonia. What forms?

choices.text: A paramagnetic blue solution containing Na(NH3)6^+ and solvated electrons
A colorless solution of NaNH2 and H2 at once
choices.why: Solvated electrons only reduce ammonia to NH2^− and H2 in the presence of a catalyst; without one, the blue solution of solvated electrons persists.

choices.text: A bronze solution of sodide ions, Na^−
choices.why: Bronze sodide solutions form at higher sodium concentrations. At low concentration the solution is blue, with solvated electrons.

choices.text: Insoluble sodium metal that sinks to the bottom
choices.why: Sodium does dissolve in dry ammonia, giving solvated cations and electrons.

explanation: Small amounts of sodium dissolve in dry donor solvents such as ammonia to give paramagnetic blue solutions of Na(NH3)6^+ and solvated electrons. At higher sodium concentrations, bronze solutions containing sodide anions, Na^−, form. Both are excellent reducing agents, able even to reduce gold to Au^−.

prompt: "Inverse sodium hydride" is formally H^+Na^−. What allows it to be isolated?

choices.text: The H^+ ion is encapsulated in an adamanzane cage, which slows its thermodynamically favorable reduction by the sodide anion
Reduction of H^+ by Na^− is thermodynamically unfavorable
choices.why: The reduction of H^+ by sodide is thermodynamically favorable. The cage slows it down kinetically.

choices.text: Sodium is more electronegative than hydrogen
choices.why: Sodium is much less electronegative. The salt survives only because the encapsulated H^+ reacts slowly.

choices.text: It is simply ordinary NaH with a different name
choices.why: Ordinary NaH contains Na^+ and H^−. Inverse sodium hydride has the charges reversed: H^+ and Na^−.

explanation: Inverse sodium hydride is formally an H^+ salt of the sodide anion. The H^+ is encapsulated in an adamanzane cage, which slows the thermodynamically favorable reduction of H^+ by Na^− enough to allow the salt to be isolated.

prompt: LiCl, NaCl, KCl, and RbCl crystallize in the rock salt structure, but CsCl, CsBr, and CsI adopt the CsCl structure. What is the reason?

choices.text: The larger Cs^+ ion can fit eight halide ions around it instead of six
Cs^+ carries a +2 charge
choices.why: Cs forms a +1 cation like the other alkali metals. The difference is its larger size.

choices.text: The smaller cations fit eight halides, while Cs^+ fits only six
choices.why: It's the reverse: the smaller cations have six halides around them (rock salt), and the larger Cs^+ has eight.

choices.text: Cesium halides are covalent molecules rather than ionic solids
choices.why: Cesium halides are ionic solids; the CsCl structure has cubic coordination of eight halides about each Cs^+.

explanation: Cation size helps determine the structure an alkali metal compound adopts. The halides of the smaller Li^+, Na^+, K^+, and Rb^+ ions take the rock salt structure, with six halides around each ion. The chlorides, bromides, and iodides of the larger Cs^+ ion adopt the CsCl structure, with eight halides at the corners of a cube around each Cs^+.

prompt: When K, Rb, and Cs are burned in an excess of oxygen, what kind of product do they form?

choices.text: 1:1 salts of the large superoxide ion, O2^−
Simple oxides, M2O, like most metals
choices.why: Most metals do form oxides, but the larger alkali metals favor the larger superoxide ion.

choices.text: Nitrides, M3N
choices.why: Burning in excess oxygen gives oxygen compounds. Among the alkali metals, only Li forms a stable nitride.

choices.text: 2:1 salts of the oxide ion, O^2−
choices.why: The larger alkali metals favor larger anions: K, Rb, and Cs give superoxides, MO2.

explanation: Size effects are believed to explain the alkali metals' unusual tendency to form peroxides and superoxides. While most metals give oxides, Li and Na also form 2:1 salts of the larger peroxide ion (O2^2−), and K, Rb, and Cs form 1:1 salts of the similarly large superoxide ion (O2^−).

prompt: 18-crown-6 has a cavity diameter of 2.6–3.2 Å. Which alkali metal ion does it bind preferentially?

choices.text: K^+ (cation diameter 2.66 Å)
Li^+ (cation diameter 1.36 Å)
choices.why: Li^+ is far smaller than the cavity; it is matched by 14-crown-4.

choices.text: Na^+ (cation diameter 1.94 Å)
choices.why: Na^+ fits the smaller cavity of 15-crown-5 best.

choices.text: Cs^+ (cation diameter 3.34 Å)
choices.why: Cs^+ is larger than this cavity; it is matched by 21-crown-7.

explanation: Crown ethers prefer cations whose size matches their binding cavity: 14-crown-4 binds Li^+, 15-crown-5 binds Na^+, 18-crown-6 binds K^+, and 21-crown-7 binds Cs^+. The 2.66 Å K^+ ion fits the 2.6–3.2 Å cavity of 18-crown-6.

prompt: Crown ethers are named x-crown-y, where x is the total number of atoms in the ring and y is the number of oxygen atoms; the rest of the ring atoms are carbon. How many carbon atoms are in the ring of 15-crown-5?
explanation: The ring has 15 atoms in total, 5 of them oxygen, so it has 15 − 5 = 10 carbon atoms. (Likewise, 18-crown-6 has 6 O and 12 C.)

prompt: Why are cavity-size estimates only of limited use in predicting how strongly a cryptand binds different alkali metal ions?

choices.text: Cryptands are flexible, so their O and N donor sites can shift to accommodate ions, even ones nominally too large for the cavity
Cryptands bind only one alkali metal ion and no others
choices.why: All four cryptands discussed can bind all the alkali metals; their flexibility lets them adjust.

choices.text: Cryptands bind metals only through their carbon atoms
choices.why: Cryptands bind through their oxygen and nitrogen Lewis base sites.

choices.text: Cryptand cavities change size with the solvent's pH
choices.why: The section attributes the limited predictive value to the ring's conformational flexibility, not to pH.

explanation: Cryptands, like crown ethers, tend to prefer ions whose size matches their cavity, but their ring systems are flexible. Their O and N donor sites can adjust position to fit each ion, so all the cryptands can bind all the alkali metals, and one cryptand was found to prefer the smaller Rb^+ over Cs^+ contrary to the simple size prediction.
